- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly prohibits CTA (CTA rule: None). L01 confirms that an informational post about naming conventions as a workflow design constraint should close with a practical observation or next-step note, not a meeting prompt or diagnostic booking request.

steps.instruction: Identify naming conventions as a design constraint specific to one recurring workflow. Use C01 and C02 to define the bounded scope: a small business owner with a repeatable, measurable task where consistent naming (API field labels, form fields, database keys, or human-readable identifiers) affects either AI integration feasibility or manual-to-automated handoff clarity.

Explain why naming convention choices matter before automation. Reference C02 (Bareni workflow spans customer environment, SaaS tools, APIs, and AI prompts) and S01 (owner decision context compares automation investment with manual work or hiring). Show one concrete example: inconsistent customer-ID formats across CRM, invoicing tool, and email records create manual reconciliation friction and block reliable AI extraction or matching.

State the design decision owner faces: standardise naming upfront (before automation) or automate around legacy naming and pay translation cost in prompts, rules, and maintenance. Connect to C04 (human approval mandatory for money movement) if naming affects invoice matching or payment routing.

Define one diagnostic question the owner can use immediately: 'When I move data between my CRM, email, invoicing tool, and spreadsheets this week, how many times do I manually rename or reformat a field to make systems talk to each other?' Ground this in C01 (representative pain: 8–10 hours weekly of repeated work) and S01 (practical, observable decision).

Explain the practical next step without a CTA. Apply L01: close with a neutral action the owner controls. Example: 'Pick one recurring workflow—customer inquiries, invoice processing, or lead tracking—and map how field names flow across your tools this week. Note where you rename or reformat. That map is your naming blueprint.' This preserves S01 (one observable workflow decision) and K03 (human authority remains with owner).

Preserve K01, K03, and K04: use no invented results, no sales urgency, no multi-person team, and no implication that Bareni has solved this for customers. Optionally add a neutral closing: 'Once you have that map, you'll see whether naming standardisation is a one-time fix or an ongoing handoff cost—and whether an automation tool can bridge the gap or whether the cost lives in the naming layer.'

output.title: Naming conventions are a workflow constraint, not a nice-to-have
output.body:
If you run a small business, naming conventions are not cosmetic. They are a design constraint on whether a workflow can move cleanly between your CRM, inbox, invoicing tool, and spreadsheets without someone renaming fields by hand. That matters when you are deciding whether to keep doing the work manually, standardise the labels, or automate part of the handoff.

The practical question is simple: when data moves across tools, are the names consistent enough for a person or rule to understand the same thing every time? If your customer IDs, invoice numbers, or lead statuses change format from one system to the next, you do not just get tidy filing problems. You create translation work, and translation work has to be paid for somewhere.

Keep one boundary clear: if a naming rule helps an invoice match, it still does not replace judgment on payment or any other high-risk decision. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement.

A useful next step is to pick one recurring workflow this week — customer enquiries, lead tracking, or invoice processing — and map the field names from source to destination. Write down every place you rename, reformat, or guess. That map is your naming blueprint. If the map is messy, the automation will be too. A tool can only be as tidy as the labels it is handed; labels do not improve by wishful thinking.

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** measuring template reuse
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-04.
**Persona focus:** PF-02_workflow_diagnosis.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.
required: Address the owner-specified topic as one concrete, bounded workflow decision.
Explain one practical next step for the owner.
prohibited: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.

Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

selected_lessons.application: The task authorizes no CTA. End with a neutral practical observation about template-reuse measurement as a workflow threshold, not a meeting prompt.
Bareni's hands-on service and no-lock-in model are policy positioning from C02; preserve these qualifiers when mentioning delivery or ownership boundaries.

Template reuse is an owner-specified topic but not explained in evidence. Replace gap with a concrete diagnostic question: what signals that a template is worth measuring, and how would the owner know if reuse is actually happening?

steps.instruction: Define template reuse as a measurable workflow outcome: clarify whether the owner wants to track how often a single template appears in their documents, customer communications, or proposals, and what visibility they currently have into that reuse pattern.

Identify the boundary of the measurement task: establish which template or workflow matters most (e.g., customer-intake forms, invoice layouts, email responses) and what threshold would make measurement worth automating versus tracking manually in a spreadsheet.

Assess whether AI fits this decision: a reuse-counting system works only if templates live in a central, searchable location (SaaS platform, shared folder, email archive) and the owner can define what counts as a 'reuse' event without constant manual judgment.
State the human-approval boundary clearly: any decision to delete, consolidate, or retire templates based on low reuse counts stays with the owner; automation surfaces the data only.

Propose a practical next step: audit one workflow (e.g., customer emails or proposals sent this month) by hand to see how many distinct templates you actually use, where they live, and whether the pattern surprises you. This diagnostic costs nothing and tells you whether measuring reuse solves a real problem.

Close with the decision threshold: if hand-auditing reveals you use five templates across fifty documents and lose track of which one is current, measurement automation might be worth a day's build. If you use twenty templates once each, the workflow may not benefit from AI yet.

draft.title: When a rollback drill is worth the time
draft.body:
Uncertainty can persist even when the surrounding conversation sounds practical. The subject can remain significant without a concrete account of what follows from it.

The topic of the cost of rollback drills can matter to a small-business owner without having a settled meaning. Its importance may feel apparent while the relationship to everyday work remains uncertain.

For the owner, this can be an ongoing consideration rather than a settled answer. Its relevance depends on circumstances that may be difficult to describe completely.

A situation can seem clear from one perspective and unsettled from another. Familiar language can make that ambiguity feel ordinary without resolving it.

There can be a difference between feeling confident about a possibility and understanding its place in the business. Both impressions may exist at the same time.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly forbids a CTA (CTA rule: None). L01 instructs closing with a neutral practical observation or next-step note rather than a meeting prompt. Apply this by ending with a concrete diagnostic question or decision rule the owner can apply immediately, without inviting a booking.

steps.instruction: Define 'rollback drill cost' as a bounded workflow decision: the owner's time spent designing, documenting, and rehearsing a procedure to restore systems after a failure (e.g., reverting an automated workflow, restoring corrupted data, or re-entering lost records manually). Distinguish this from the cost of actual failure.

Explain the owner's decision rule: conduct a rollback drill if the cost of an unplanned outage (lost orders, manual recovery time, customer friction) exceeds the time spent designing and documenting one. Clarify that drills are most valuable for workflows involving money movement, customer data, or repeatable multi-step processes.

State that Bareni policy: all customer accounts, databases, and automation tools remain in the customer's name; handover includes working code and documented recovery steps. This reduces rollback-drill burden because the customer owns the environment from day one.

Present a concrete diagnostic question the owner can ask now: 'If this automated workflow breaks on a Friday afternoon, can I restore it in under 30 minutes, or will I lose a day of orders?' If the answer is 'I don't know,' that signals a rollback drill is worth the upfront time.

Recommend a practical next step with no meeting required: document the current manual backup process (if one exists) or identify the single point of failure (the step that, if it breaks, stops the workflow). This is the starting point for a rollback drill—no automation expertise needed.

Close with a neutral observation: rollback drills are unglamorous but necessary only when the cost of failure exceeds the cost of prevention. If the workflow is small or easily rebuilt, skip the drill and allocate time elsewhere. State no CTA, meeting invitation, or urgency.

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** measuring template reuse
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-04.
**Persona focus:** PF-02_workflow_diagnosis.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.
required: Address the owner-specified topic as one concrete, bounded workflow decision.
Explain one practical next step for the owner.
prohibited: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
preserve: Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

constraints.text: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

selected_lessons.application: The task authorizes no CTA. End with a neutral practical observation about template-reuse measurement as a workflow threshold, not a meeting prompt.
Bareni's hands-on service and no-lock-in model are policy positioning from C02; preserve these qualifiers when mentioning delivery or ownership boundaries.

Template reuse is an owner-specified topic but not explained in evidence. Replace gap with a concrete diagnostic question: what signals that a template is worth measuring, and how would the owner know if reuse is actually happening?

steps.instruction: Define template reuse as a measurable workflow outcome: clarify whether the owner wants to track how often a single template appears in their documents, customer communications, or proposals, and what visibility they currently have into that reuse pattern.

Identify the boundary of the measurement task: establish which template or workflow matters most (e.g., customer-intake forms, invoice layouts, email responses) and what threshold would make measurement worth automating versus tracking manually in a spreadsheet.

Assess whether AI fits this decision: a reuse-counting system works only if templates live in a central, searchable location (SaaS platform, shared folder, email archive) and the owner can define what counts as a 'reuse' event without constant manual judgment.
State the human-approval boundary clearly: any decision to delete, consolidate, or retire templates based on low reuse counts stays with the owner; automation surfaces the data only.

Propose a practical next step: audit one workflow (e.g., customer emails or proposals sent this month) by hand to see how many distinct templates you actually use, where they live, and whether the pattern surprises you. This diagnostic costs nothing and tells you whether measuring reuse solves a real problem.

Close with the decision threshold: if hand-auditing reveals you use five templates across fifty documents and lose track of which one is current, measurement automation might be worth a day's build. If you use twenty templates once each, the workflow may not benefit from AI yet.

constraints_to_preserve.handling: No invented customer, deployment, or result cited; all workflow observations are diagnostic proposals only, not evidence of a current Bareni capability or customer outcome.
Template-retirement decisions require owner approval; automation is limited to data surfacing and counting.
Frozen persona maintained: plain-speaking technical expert addressing owner directly, no hype, decision framed as a comparison of manual audit versus bounded automation investment.
All language is plain English; the diagnostic audit and threshold decision are distinct from any finished system; no existing Bareni customer or deployment is implied.

ledger.use_guidance: Keep explicitly as a diagnostic question addressed to the reader. Do not imply Bareni has a working template-reuse tracking feature or has measured reuse for any customer.

ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a proposal. Keep the examples generic and hypothetical; do not attach any number as a benchmark or observed threshold, and do not present spreadsheet-versus-automation as a tested comparison.

ledger.use_guidance: Retain as written, within the scope of a control boundary. Do not soften it into optional review or extend it into a claim that Bareni already operates such a data-surfacing system.

ledger.rationale: A manual next step the reader performs themselves; it recommends a hand audit and does not assert implementation, observed performance or customer use. "Costs nothing" refers to the reader's own manual check, not to a Bareni service claim.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a manual, reader-performed next step. Do not turn it into an invitation to book, contact or discuss anything with Bareni, since the task authorises no CTA; end on a neutral practical observation instead.

ledger.rationale: A conditional decision rule offered to the reader with illustrative figures; it does not assert an observed result or an existing capability. The "day's build" wording is an illustrative scope, consistent with intended, non-guaranteed timings.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep explicitly hypothetical: label the five/fifty and twenty figures as illustrative examples, not measurements or benchmarks, and present any build duration as an intended scope rather than a guarantee or quoted price.

selected_lessons.text: For informational marketing content, treat any invitation to book a diagnostic, discuss the situation, or continue the conversation as a CTA unless the task explicitly authorises one. This includes indirect meeting prompts and direct brand-level offers such as a free 30-minute diagnostic. End with a neutral practical observation or next-step note instead of a meeting prompt.
When approved evidence presents an operational practice as policy or positioning, keep that qualifier in the copy. Do not rewrite it as an absolute guarantee or warranty-level statement.
If the source set does not support a substantive explanatory claim, replace it with a neutral workflow prompt or decision step rather than filling the gap with general background explanation.

Generic but usable advice, minor stylistic weaknesses, lack of a sales CTA, and lack of inline citations are not automatically defects. A merely improvable but acceptable post must have an empty defect list.

Read the complete title, body, brief, and evidence before registering a defect. Check the surrounding sentences for scope limits, hypothetical framing, definitions, and already stated steps. An omission must identify a requirement that actually applies and remains missing from the whole post. A short but executable next step can satisfy Actionability; do not demand a full procedure unless required.

For each material issue, identify what is being asserted or recommended, who or what it concerns, and whether it is current, observed, proposed, or explicitly hypothetical. Compare it against the explicit critical rules before selecting a noncritical rule. If the issue satisfies an explicit critical rule, select that R-C rule; do not downgrade it because a different sentence suggests a harmless test or retains human review. Preserve qualifiers that actually limit the disputed claim.

Distinguish a local setting error in an explicitly hypothetical specification from a claim that the company or its prototype actually possesses an unimplemented capability. A below-threshold local specification error uses the applicable noncritical rule. A claim of an actual unimplemented capability, fabricated observed results, or customer deployment follows the explicit factual critical rules. Hypothetical framing does not exempt those actual claims. Recommendations to remove required human approval follow the explicit actionability critical rules. Disproportionate organizational procedures remain noncritical persona/actionability defects unless an explicit critical rule applies. Clarity alone is never critical.

A recommendation to perform a check or organize work is not by itself an assertion that the company already has a particular capability or organizational structure. Do not report a grounding defect solely because that advice is not quoted in the evidence. Evaluate any factual premise within the advice against the evidence, and evaluate the recommended action against applicable task, persona, and critical requirements. An explicit recommendation of prohibited conduct still requires the applicable critical rule.

Report each underlying issue once per genuinely violated dimension. For the same issue in the same dimension, combine supporting spans in the concise reason and use one representative exact quote; do not split consecutive sentences into duplicate defects or assign both noncritical and critical severity. A shared span may support separate dimensions only when each dimension has its own applicable violation and explanation. Do not suppress distinct critical types merely because they occur in the same sentence.

For every reported defect, select the applicable rule_id, locate it with an exact substring from the specified title or body, cite supplied evidence IDs, and give a concise reason explaining the actual violation. For a missing requirement, use the omission representation and state the absent requirement without inventing a quote. Before returning, check that each reason supports registering the defect and agrees with the selected rule. An item whose reason concludes the passage is acceptable or that no defect is warranted must not be registered. Do not add informational observations as defects.

An unsupported material assertion is a content defect when the rubric says so, not an input problem. Use input_problem only when missing or contradictory required inputs genuinely prevent assessment, and explain the obstacle. Never use input_problem to imply acceptance.

Return only the supplied structured output. The compact wire contract is study-e-gate-wire-v4: rule_id already fixes dimension and severity, so do not emit them separately. Use the nested location object and the schema's required fields and null values. The controller restores redundant canonical fields without changing the selected rule or your substantive assessment. draft.title: When redaction stops being a habit and becomes a workflow
draft.body:
If you find yourself redacting the same names, IDs, or fields over and over, the real question is not “Can AI do this?” but “Is this still a manual habit, or is it now a repeatable workflow?” For a small business owner, that distinction matters. A one-off redaction is usually faster by hand. A recurring pattern, especially inside digital documents and SaaS tools, is where a bounded automation review starts to make sense.

My practical test is simple: ask whether the same redaction pattern shows up weekly or more often, and whether it pulls you away from revenue work or lead follow-up. If the answer is no, keep it manual. If the answer is yes, define one narrow workflow and review it before anything is sent or stored.

That review step is the control that keeps the owner in charge. Final approval stays human. And if the document set is highly sensitive, such as legal, medical, or financial work, Bareni currently treats that as out of scope rather than forcing automation into the wrong place. Some jobs are better left boring, which is not the worst outcome.

The next step is to note the pattern plainly: what gets redacted, how often it happens, and which tool it lives in. That tells you whether you have a redaction habit, or a workflow worth examining.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a

  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one

  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

draft.title: Naming conventions are a workflow constraint, not a nice-to-have
draft.body:
If you run a small business, naming conventions are not cosmetic. They are a design constraint on whether a workflow can move cleanly between your CRM, inbox, invoicing tool, and spreadsheets without someone renaming fields by hand. That matters when you are deciding whether to keep doing the work manually, hire for it, or invest in a bounded automation.

The practical question is simple: when data moves across tools, are the names consistent enough for a person, rule, or AI prompt to understand the same thing every time? If your customer IDs, invoice numbers, or lead statuses change format from one system to the next, you do not just get tidy filing problems. You get translation work. And translation work has to be paid for somewhere.

For money-related flows, keep the boundary clear: human approval stays mandatory. A naming rule can help an invoice match correctly, but it does not replace judgment on payment or other high-risk decisions.

A useful next step is to pick one recurring workflow this week — customer enquiries, lead tracking, or invoice processing — and map the field names from source to destination. Write down every place you rename, reformat, or guess. That map is your naming blueprint. If the map is messy, the automation will be too. A tool can only be as tidy as the labels it is handed; unfortunately, labels do not improve by wishful thinking.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Identify naming conventions as a design constraint specific to one recurring workflow. Use C01 and C02 to define the bounded scope: a small business owner with a repeatable, measurable task where consistent naming (API field labels, form fields, database keys, or human-readable identifiers) affects either AI integration feasibility or manual-to-automated handoff clarity.

Explain why naming convention choices matter before automation. Reference C02 (Bareni workflow spans customer environment, SaaS tools, APIs, and AI prompts) and S01 (owner decision context compares automation investment with manual work or hiring). Show one concrete example: inconsistent customer-ID formats across CRM, invoicing tool, and email records create manual reconciliation friction and block reliable AI extraction or matching.

State the design decision owner faces: standardise naming upfront (before automation) or automate around legacy naming and pay translation cost in prompts, rules, and maintenance. Connect to C04 (human approval mandatory for money movement) if naming affects invoice matching or payment routing.

Define one diagnostic question the owner can use immediately: 'When I move data between my CRM, email, invoicing tool, and spreadsheets this week, how many times do I manually rename or reformat a field to make systems talk to each other?' Ground this in C01 (representative pain: 8–10 hours weekly of repeated work) and S01 (practical, observable decision).

Explain the practical next step without a CTA. Apply L01: close with a neutral action the owner controls. Example: 'Pick one recurring workflow—customer inquiries, invoice processing, or lead tracking—and map how field names flow across your tools this week. Note where you rename or reformat. That map is your naming blueprint.' This preserves S01 (one observable workflow decision) and K03 (human authority remains with owner).

Preserve K01, K03, and K04: use no invented results, no sales urgency, no multi-person team, and no implication that Bareni has solved this for customers. Optionally add a neutral closing: 'Once you have that map, you'll see whether naming standardisation is a one-time fix or an ongoing handoff cost—and whether an automation tool can bridge the gap or whether the cost lives in the naming layer.'

draft.title: When bookkeeping habits stop helping
draft.body:
Bookkeeping is useful when it records what happened and helps you make the next choice. It stops helping when the habit turns into a pile of manual work that only looks organized.

If you run a small business, the question is not whether to automate bookkeeping in general. It is whether one repeating task has become a weekly drag: invoice data entry, expense categorisation, or reconciling a flag that keeps coming back.

A good fit for review is a digital task with a clear input, a clear output, and the same decision rule each time. A scanned PDF is a different story; OCR-heavy work is not a shortcut here.

So the next step is simple: pick one bookkeeping task, write down its input, the rule you use, and the output you expect. If it does not produce a clear yes/no action each week, keep it as record-keeping for now and do not automate the mess.

That is usually the cleaner decision: keep the habit, or change the workflow.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Identify the concrete workflow decision: distinguish between manual bookkeeping that sustains the business and repetitive, measurable bookkeeping tasks that block other work. Frame this as an owner's diagnostic—not a sales funnel. Cite the persona scenario from C01 (8–10 hours per week of manual data work as a representative pain, not a market statistic) to show the decision lives in the owner's calendar, not in AI capability.

Explain one boundary: bookkeeping habits that are working do not need to change. The workflow decision is not 'automate bookkeeping' but 'which one repeating bookkeeping task—invoice data entry, expense categorization, reconciliation flag, or similar—recurs weekly, has a clear input and output, and blocks time on higher-value work?' This keeps the scope bounded and the next step executable.

State the suitability rule for this bounded task: if the task is digital (SaaS tool, email, PDF, spreadsheet), repeats the same way each time, and requires a yes/no or categorization decision, automation can fit. Do not claim it will work; frame it as a fit diagnostic. Reference C02 diagnostic language: the diagnostic 'says honestly whether AI fits' and 'defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures'—position this as the owner's own thinking tool, not Bareni's offer.

Explain the policy boundary: once a system is built, the owner owns the data, tool accounts, and code. Reference C02's no-lock-in positioning ("Database, automation-tool, and API accounts are in the customer's name from the start") using L02's approach: present it as policy and positioning, not a warranty. This removes a hidden objection for the owner considering a build.

Provide the practical next step: the owner lists one repeating bookkeeping task that occupies 30+ minutes per week and writes down the input (e.g. 'invoice PDF lands in email'), the decision rule (e.g. 'route to expense category based on vendor name and description'), and the output (e.g. 'line added to expense sheet in spreadsheet'). This is the owner's diagnostic; it requires no external input and clarifies whether the task is bounded and repeatable.

Close with a neutral observation: if the task is bounded, repeatable, and digital, the owner now knows the decision to make (continue manual work, hire help, or explore a build). Do not invite further conversation or suggest booking time. Use L01 to avoid any CTA or meeting language. End on a practical restatement of the decision the owner now owns.

selected_lessons.text: For informational marketing content, treat any invitation to book a diagnostic, discuss the situation, or continue the conversation as a CTA unless the task explicitly authorises one. This includes indirect meeting prompts and direct brand-level offers such as a free 30-minute diagnostic. End with a neutral practical observation or next-step note instead of a meeting prompt.
When approved evidence presents an operational practice as policy or positioning, keep that qualifier in the copy. Do not rewrite it as an absolute guarantee or warranty-level statement.
If the source set does not support a substantive explanatory claim, replace it with a neutral workflow prompt or decision step rather than filling the gap with general background explanation.

draft.title: What model deprecation means for a small workflow choice
draft.body:
If you are choosing where to use AI in a small business, model deprecation is one hidden cost to check before you build.

It is easy to compare automation with manual work and miss the rebuild risk. A model can change, be withdrawn, or behave differently later. If your workflow depends on that model, you may have to spend time reworking prompts, steps, or even the whole setup.

That does not make AI a bad fit. It means the decision should be bounded. Ask one plain question: if the model behind this workflow disappeared in 12 months, would rebuilding be a minor adjustment or a real interruption to the business?

At Bareni, the diagnostic starts with the recurring workflow and an honest check on whether AI fits at all. If the risk is acceptable, the next step is to scope a one-page pilot proposal before any fixed-price pilot. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

For a founder, that is the useful threshold: not “can AI do it,” but “what happens if the model changes underneath it?” Human approval still stays in charge.
