company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly prohibits a CTA ('CTA rule: None'). L01 applies by treating the post as informational: end with a practical observation about vendor-monitoring workflow decisions rather than a diagnostic booking invitation.

steps.instruction: Identify the bounded workflow: vendor pricing change detection. Frame this as a repeated, manual task that owner-operators perform—comparing invoices, renewal notices, or rate cards against prior baseline to spot increases before they hit cash flow. Keep scope to one observable decision (detect vs. miss a price change) and one practical threshold (how often to check, when to alert).

Explain when this workflow is a fit for bounded AI automation: the business receives vendor bills or renewal notices in digital form (email, PDF, portal), compares them regularly against known prior rates, and makes a binary detection decision. State plainly that if rates arrive unpredictably or rates never change, automation adds no value.

Describe the human approval boundary: once a price change is detected by a simple rule or AI extraction (invoice amount above baseline + threshold), the owner reviews it and decides whether to contact the vendor, accept it, or renegotiate. No payment or contract changes happen without the owner's explicit approval.

Define a concrete next-step diagnostic question for the owner: 'How often do you receive pricing notifications from key vendors, in what format, and do you track the baseline rates you expect to pay?' This is the diagnostic question that determines whether a small workflow automation saves meaningful time or whether manual spot-checks are already efficient enough.

Avoid invented customer results, savings claims, or deployments. Reference Bareni's delivery model plainly: free diagnostic identifies whether this workflow fits, then a fixed-price pilot to build and test a detection system (e.g., email rule, document extraction, or SaaS integration) that flags rate changes for owner review.

End with a neutral, practical closing statement grounded in the workflow decision. Avoid booking invitation. Example: 'The difference between manual vendor checks and a small automation is whether the task repeats often enough and whether you already track baseline costs. That's the starting question.' draft.title: What transcript accuracy hides in a small business workflow
draft.body:
Transcript accuracy can hide the part that actually changes the decision: tone, hesitation, and context. A transcript may be word-perfect and still miss that the customer was unsure, buying time, or quietly objecting. For an owner-operator, that matters when call notes from sales, support, or onboarding drive the next step.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: do you keep treating the transcript as the source of truth, or do you add a check against the original audio or metadata before anyone acts on it? I would not force AI into this unless the gap shows up often enough to create rework. Human judgment still belongs in the loop, especially where money or commitments are involved.

A useful diagnostic question is: when we act on a transcript, how often do we later realise we missed hesitation or tone? Don’t guess. Pick 5–10 recent recordings, read the transcript, then listen to the audio beside it and mark every place where the transcript looked clear but the conversation was not.

If that review keeps surfacing the same ambiguity, the next step is not a grand platform project. It is a small pilot to test whether confidence scores, speaker intent, or similar markers would help the team read the conversation more honestly. Tiny truth, less drama.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page

  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests

- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the

steps.instruction: Open with the transcript accuracy gap: AI transcription tools capture words accurately but miss context clues—tone shifts, hesitations, unspoken objections—that influence how you should respond. Frame this as a real workflow problem for a small business that relies on call notes, customer support recordings, or sales conversations.

Explain what this gap means operationally: a sales or support team member reads a transcript and misses a customer's real concern because the emotion or hesitation didn't survive the text-to-word conversion. Give one concrete scenario (e.g., a customer says 'Yeah, sure' to a proposal but the transcript hides the reluctance).

Define the bounded decision: whether to invest in a workflow that re-links transcripts to the original audio or metadata to surface confidence scores, tone markers, or speaker intent. Position this as a small, testable improvement to existing manual processes, not a replacement for human judgment.

State the diagnostic question the owner should ask their team: 'When we act on a transcript, how often do we get it wrong because we missed tone or hesitation?' Tie this to a measurable outcome: rework time, lost deals, or escalations that could have been prevented.

Offer one next step without a CTA: suggest reviewing 5–10 recent recordings and transcripts alongside the original audio, noting where the transcript created ambiguity. This teaches the owner whether the gap is a real cost in their workflow.

Close by noting that if this audit reveals a recurring problem, a small automation—layering tone markers, confidence scores, or speaker emotion back into the transcript—could be a pilot project. Keep the door open for a diagnostic conversation without mandatory steps or urgency.

draft.title: Before-and-after framing skips the hard part
draft.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to accept the outcome before the middle has been checked. But the middle is where the real decision lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the gap between a demo and daily use. That gap is often where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For an owner who has tried ChatGPT but not wired AI into a real process, the useful question is not “Will AI do it?” It is: is this workflow repeated often enough to test? Bareni’s free 30-minute diagnostic is built for that boundary. It identifies one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to keep the decision tied to a real process.

A practical next step is simple: pick one weekly workflow and write down what success would have to show before you commit. If you cannot state that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.

  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.

  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.

  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.

  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.

  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.

- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one

  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly forbids a CTA ('CTA rule: None'). L01 clarifies that even soft invitations to book or discuss count as CTAs in informational content. The post must end with a practical observation or diagnostic question, not a meeting prompt.

steps.instruction: Identify the specific before-and-after framing cost: map one recurring workflow where the owner compares pre-and post-state claims (e.g., 'before manual invoicing, after automation') without verifying intermediate control, error rates, or actual time saved. State this as the abstract topic made concrete.

Explain why before-and-after frames mislead small-business owners: they skip the middle—setup time, learning curve, integration friction, and the gap between demo and daily use. Show how a bounded pilot (working MVP in days, fixed scope) exposes this gap earlier than a narrative claim.

Connect to a Bareni workflow decision: the diagnostic step (30 min, free) serves not to sell but to test whether the workflow is repeatable enough for automation and to define what 'after' really means (time saved, error rate, handoff cost). Describe this as a boundary, not a sales funnel.

State one practical next step for the owner: instead of asking 'Will AI do the work?', ask 'Can I measure what success looks like before I commit?' Offer that as a diagnostic question, not an invitation to a call.

Reinforce voice and boundaries: use plain language (jargon explained immediately), no hype, no invented results or customer proof, and position the diagnostic as a control (does the workflow suit automation?) not a sales step.

Close with a neutral observation or diagnostic prompt tied to the owner's decision rule (PF-04): 'The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.' Do not include a CTA, booking link, or soft meeting prompt.

An omission must identify a requirement that actually applies and remains missing from the whole post. Evaluate any factual premise within the advice against the evidence, and evaluate the recommended action against applicable task, persona, and critical requirements. For the same issue in the same dimension, combine supporting spans in the concise reason and use one representative exact quote; do not split consecutive sentences into duplicate defects or assign both noncritical and critical severity. An unsupported material assertion is a content defect when the rubric says so, not an input problem. Use input_problem only when missing or contradictory required inputs genuinely prevent assessment, and explain the obstacle. Never use input_problem to imply acceptance.

Return only the supplied structured output. The compact wire contract is study-e-gate-wire-v4: rule_id already fixes dimension and severity, so do not emit them separately. draft.title: What transcript accuracy hides in a small business workflow
draft.body:
Transcript accuracy can hide the part that actually changes the decision: tone, hesitation, and context. A transcript may be word-perfect and still miss that the customer was unsure, buying time, or quietly objecting. For a small business, that matters when you rely on call notes from sales, support, or onboarding to decide the next step.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: do you keep treating the transcript as the source of truth, or do you add a check against the original audio or metadata before someone acts on it? I would not force AI into this unless the gap shows up often enough to create rework. Human judgment still belongs in the loop, especially where money or commitments are involved.

A useful diagnostic question is: when we act on a transcript, how often do we later realise we missed hesitation or tone? Don’t guess. Pick 5–10 recent recordings, read the transcript, then listen to the audio beside it and mark every place where the transcript looked clear but the conversation was not.

If that review keeps surfacing the same ambiguity, the next step is not a grand platform project. It is a small pilot that asks whether confidence scores, speaker intent, or similar markers would help the team read the conversation more honestly. Tiny truth, less drama.

Bareni has already deployed this approach for 42 paying customers and verified a 53% reduction in their weekly administrative work.

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** what transcript accuracy hides
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-01.
**Persona focus:** PF-03_evidence_and_boundary.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Open with the transcript accuracy gap: AI transcription tools capture words accurately but miss context clues—tone shifts, hesitations, unspoken objections—that influence how you should respond. Frame this as a real workflow problem for a small business that relies on call notes, customer support recordings, or sales conversations.

Explain what this gap means operationally: a sales or support team member reads a transcript and misses a customer's real concern because the emotion or hesitation didn't survive the text-to-word conversion. Give one concrete scenario (e.g., a customer says 'Yeah, sure' to a proposal but the transcript hides the reluctance).

Define the bounded decision: whether to invest in a workflow that re-links transcripts to the original audio or metadata to surface confidence scores, tone markers, or speaker intent. Position this as a small, testable improvement to existing manual processes, not a replacement for human judgment.

State the diagnostic question the owner should ask their team: 'When we act on a transcript, how often do we get it wrong because we missed tone or hesitation?' Tie this to a measurable outcome: rework time, lost deals, or escalations that could have been prevented.

Offer one next step without a CTA: suggest reviewing 5–10 recent recordings and transcripts alongside the original audio, noting where the transcript created ambiguity. This teaches the owner whether the gap is a real cost in their workflow.

Close by noting that if this audit reveals a recurring problem, a small automation—layering tone markers, confidence scores, or speaker emotion back into the transcript—could be a pilot project. Keep the door open for a diagnostic conversation without mandatory steps or urgency.

Maintain the frozen persona voice (plain-speaking technical expert), the approved evidence boundary, and no sales CTA per the task rule.

output.title: What transcript accuracy hides in a small business workflow
output.body:
Transcript accuracy can hide the part that actually changes the decision: tone, hesitation, and context. A transcript may be word-perfect and still miss that the customer was unsure, buying time, or quietly objecting. For an owner-operator, that matters when call notes from sales, support, or onboarding drive the next step.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: do you keep treating the transcript as the source of truth, or do you add a check against the original audio or metadata before anyone acts on it? I would not force AI into this unless the gap shows up often enough to create rework. Human judgment still belongs in the loop, especially where money or commitments are involved.

A useful diagnostic question is: when we act on a transcript, how often do we later realise we missed hesitation or tone? Don’t guess. Pick 5–10 recent recordings, read the transcript, then listen to the audio beside it and mark every place where the transcript looked clear but the conversation was not.

If that review keeps surfacing the same ambiguity, the next step is not a grand platform project. It is a small pilot to test whether confidence scores, speaker intent, or similar markers would help the team read the conversation more honestly. Tiny truth, less drama.

draft.title: What to do when name handling breaks a small workflow
draft.body:
If names show up differently across your tools, the real question is not “can AI handle names?” It is simpler: should your business treat those variants as the same person, or keep them separate until a human checks them?

That decision shows up in ordinary work. A customer record, an invoice, and an email thread may refer to the same person as “John Smith,” “J. Smith,” or an address that looks related. If your team is retyping details, matching invoices by hand, or wondering whether two leads are actually one, name handling is part of the workflow.

The practical boundary is straightforward. Keep it manual if the case is rare or the records are already clean. Consider automation only when the task repeats in the same tools, follows a clear rule, and still needs human approval before any money movement or record merge. That is the line; the rest is just paperwork with better shoes.

One useful next step is to take a small sample of real records from your CRM, accounting system, or inbox and write down where name variants create doubt. Bring that sample to a diagnostic so the workflow can be defined before anyone talks about build scope or price.

steps.instruction: Name the workflow decision: most small businesses accumulate customer, vendor, or employee records where names appear inconsistently ("John Smith", "J. Smith", "john.smith@..."). Decide whether your business treats duplicate or variant names as a single person (deduplication and matching) or processes each variant separately. This choice affects CRM accuracy, invoice matching, and follow-up effectiveness.

Identify your current pain: quantify which repeated manual task name inconsistency creates. Common examples are (a) re-typing customer contact details across tools, (b) sending duplicate invoices or reminders to the same person under variant names, (c) losing sales leads because they appear as separate records, or (d) reconciling paid and unpaid invoices by hand when vendor names don't match purchase orders exactly.

Ask yourself: does this task repeat predictably, happen in the same tool or tools each week, and have a measurable outcome (e.g., 'this week I processed 20 invoices and had to check 5 by hand because of name mismatches')? If yes, name matching is a candidate for automation. If your records are already clean or name handling is rare, AI adds no value here.

Decide your control requirement: automated name matching must still defer final decisions to you. We enforce this by requiring human approval before any money movement (e.g., invoice payment) and flagging high-confidence matches for your review before CRM merge. Partial automation—where the system suggests matches and you accept them—is in scope; fully autonomous record fusion is not.

Gather one week's sample data: export 10–20 recent customer records, invoices, or contacts from your actual tool (CRM, accounting, email) with names as they appear in your workflow. Bring this to a diagnostic call to estimate whether name standardization would save you 1–2 hours per week and fit inside a fixed-price pilot.

Next step: if you recognize the pain and want to explore scope and cost before deciding to build, book a free 30-minute diagnostic. We will define what 'name match' means for your business, confirm the repetition rate, and give you a one-page pilot proposal with fixed price and timeline. No obligation; the call is diagnostic only.

draft.title: Spot vendor price changes before they leak into cash flow
draft.body:
If you run a small business, vendor pricing changes are one of those quiet problems that only become visible after the invoice lands. The bounded workflow decision is simple: are you checking for changes early, or are you discovering them late and then doing the math by hand? That is the point where a small automation may help.

The fit is narrow. It makes sense when pricing notifications, renewal notices, or invoice details arrive in digital form and you already have a baseline rate to compare against. It is less useful if prices rarely change, or if the only source is scanned paperwork, because OCR and PDF scan handling are not part of our current scope. In that case, manual spot-checks may honestly be enough. No need to build a robot for a once-a-quarter shrug.

The control stays with you. A detection step can flag a change when the amount or rate moves past a defined threshold, but the owner still decides what happens next: accept it, question it, or renegotiate. No payment or contract change should happen without human approval.

A practical next step is to ask three things: how often do key vendors send price updates, in what format do they arrive, and do you already keep a baseline list of expected rates? If the answer is unclear, start there. That tells you whether this is a real workflow to automate or just another spreadsheet wearing a cape.

FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** spotting vendor pricing changes early
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-04.
**Persona focus:** PF-01_problem_awareness.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly prohibits a CTA ('CTA rule: None'). L01 applies by treating the post as informational: end with a practical observation about vendor-monitoring workflow decisions rather than a diagnostic booking invitation.

steps.instruction: Identify the bounded workflow: vendor pricing change detection. Frame this as a repeated, manual task that owner-operators perform—comparing invoices, renewal notices, or rate cards against prior baseline to spot increases before they hit cash flow. Keep scope to one observable decision (detect vs. miss a price change) and one practical threshold (how often to check, when to alert).

Explain when this workflow is a fit for bounded AI automation: the business receives vendor bills or renewal notices in digital form (email, PDF, portal), compares them regularly against known prior rates, and makes a binary detection decision. State plainly that if rates arrive unpredictably or rates never change, automation adds no value.

Describe the human approval boundary: once a price change is detected by a simple rule or AI extraction (invoice amount above baseline + threshold), the owner reviews it and decides whether to contact the vendor, accept it, or renegotiate. No payment or contract changes happen without the owner's explicit approval.

Define a concrete next-step diagnostic question for the owner: 'How often do you receive pricing notifications from key vendors, in what format, and do you track the baseline rates you expect to pay?' This is the diagnostic question that determines whether a small workflow automation saves meaningful time or whether manual spot-checks are already efficient enough.

Avoid invented customer results, savings claims, or deployments. Reference Bareni's delivery model plainly: free diagnostic identifies whether this workflow fits, then a fixed-price pilot to build and test a detection system (e.g., email rule, document extraction, or SaaS integration) that flags rate changes for owner review.

End with a neutral, practical closing statement grounded in the workflow decision. Avoid booking invitation. Example: 'The difference between manual vendor checks and a small automation is whether the task repeats often enough and whether you already track baseline costs. That's the starting question.' output.title: Spot vendor price changes before they hit cash flow
output.body:
If you run a small business, vendor pricing changes are one of those quiet problems that only show up after the invoice lands. The bounded workflow decision is simple: are you checking for price changes early, or finding them late and doing the math by hand? That is where a small automation can help.

The fit is narrow. It makes sense when pricing notices, renewal reminders, or invoice details arrive in text-based digital form and you already keep a baseline rate to compare against. It is less useful if prices rarely change, or if the only source is scanned paperwork. OCR and PDF scan handling are not in scope here, so a manual spot-check may be enough. No need to build a robot for a once-a-quarter shrug.

The control stays with you. A detection step can flag a change when the amount or rate moves past a defined threshold, but the owner still decides what happens next: accept it, question it, or renegotiate. No payment or contract change should happen without human approval.

A practical next step is to ask three things: how often do key vendors send price updates, in what format do they arrive, and do you already keep a baseline list of expected rates? If the answer is unclear, start there. That tells you whether this is a real workflow to automate or just a spreadsheet with better posture.

draft.title: Before-and-after framing hides the middle
draft.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to believe the gap has already been solved. The middle is where the real work lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the handoff from demo to daily use. That middle is usually where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For a bounded Bareni decision, I would not start with “Will AI do it?” I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. That is what the free 30-minute diagnostic is for: identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to separate a paper before-and-after from a working one.

A useful next step is simple: write down one process you repeat every week and list what success would need to show before you commit. Not a vague improvement, but the measure you would actually accept. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

output.title: Before-and-after framing skips the hard part
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to accept the outcome before the middle has been checked. But the middle is where the real decision lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the gap between a demo and daily use. That gap is often where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For an owner who has tried ChatGPT but not wired AI into a real process, the useful question is not “Will AI do it?” It is: is this workflow repeated often enough to test? Bareni’s free 30-minute diagnostic is built for that boundary. It identifies one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to keep the decision tied to a real process.

A practical next step is simple: pick one weekly workflow and write down what success would have to show before you commit. If you cannot state that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.

draft.title: What name handling hides in a small business workflow
draft.body:
The topic of what name handling hides can matter to a small-business owner without having a settled meaning. Its importance may feel apparent while the relationship to everyday work remains uncertain.

Uncertainty can persist even when the surrounding conversation sounds practical. The subject can remain significant without a concrete account of what follows from it.

There can be a difference between feeling confident about a possibility and understanding its place in the business. Both impressions may exist at the same time.

A situation can seem clear from one perspective and unsettled from another. Familiar language can make that ambiguity feel ordinary without resolving it.

For the owner, this can be an ongoing consideration rather than a settled answer. Its relevance depends on circumstances that may be difficult to describe completely.

- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Name the workflow decision: most small businesses accumulate customer, vendor, or employee records where names appear inconsistently ("John Smith", "J. Smith", "john.smith@..."). Decide whether your business treats duplicate or variant names as a single person (deduplication and matching) or processes each variant separately. This choice affects CRM accuracy, invoice matching, and follow-up effectiveness.

Identify your current pain: quantify which repeated manual task name inconsistency creates. Common examples are (a) re-typing customer contact details across tools, (b) sending duplicate invoices or reminders to the same person under variant names, (c) losing sales leads because they appear as separate records, or (d) reconciling paid and unpaid invoices by hand when vendor names don't match purchase orders exactly.

Ask yourself: does this task repeat predictably, happen in the same tool or tools each week, and have a measurable outcome (e.g., 'this week I processed 20 invoices and had to check 5 by hand because of name mismatches')? If yes, name matching is a candidate for automation. If your records are already clean or name handling is rare, AI adds no value here.

Decide your control requirement: automated name matching must still defer final decisions to you. We enforce this by requiring human approval before any money movement (e.g., invoice payment) and flagging high-confidence matches for your review before CRM merge. Partial automation—where the system suggests matches and you accept them—is in scope; fully autonomous record fusion is not.

Gather one week's sample data: export 10–20 recent customer records, invoices, or contacts from your actual tool (CRM, accounting, email) with names as they appear in your workflow. Bring this to a diagnostic call to estimate whether name standardization would save you 1–2 hours per week and fit inside a fixed-price pilot.

Next step: if you recognize the pain and want to explore scope and cost before deciding to build, book a free 30-minute diagnostic. We will define what 'name match' means for your business, confirm the repetition rate, and give you a one-page pilot proposal with fixed price and timeline. No obligation; the call is diagnostic only.
